title: Checkpoint: Rock and Pop
objective: After this level you can trace popular music from the phonograph to the music video.
summary: The National Recording Registry adds 25 recordings a year, each at least 10 years old, and holds this chapter's story, from Scott's phonautograms to Rocket 88, Elvis at Sun, Respect and Sgt. Pepper.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: the sounds America decided never to lose.
cards.body: The Library of Congress keeps a list of recordings worth saving for good. Walk through it and you'll bump into this whole chapter, from a sheet of soot-covered paper to a Beatles album. Here's how the list works, and what it says about the road from phonograph to music video.

cards.fact: Each year the Librarian of Congress adds 25 recordings to the National Recording Registry.
cards.context: The registry comes from the National Recording Preservation Act of 2000. A recording must be at least 10 years old and "culturally, historically or aesthetically significant." So this year's biggest new hit, however huge, will have to wait its turn.

events.label: Scott's phonautograms, including "Au Clair de la Lune"

cards.headline: The chapter in one breath
cards.body: Edison's phonograph let sound be stored and played back. Radio sent one performance into millions of homes at once. Rock and roll merged rhythm and blues with country, led by Black pioneers. The electric guitar's pickup turned vibrating strings into a signal an amplifier could make loud. And MTV made how a song looked as important as how it sounded. Each new machine changed who could hear music, and how.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete

Where rock and roll came from: rhythm and blues, gospel and country, led by Black pioneers.
How an electric guitar's pickup turns a vibrating string into a signal an amplifier makes loud.
Why the power chord leaves out the third, and why that keeps it clear through distortion.

questions.prompt: How many recordings does the Librarian of Congress add to the National Recording Registry each year?

options.rationale: Many more are chosen each year.
Ten is the minimum age in years, not the yearly count.
Far fewer; the registry grows by a set number a year.

questions.explanation: Under the National Recording Preservation Act of 2000, 25 recordings are added each year.

questions.prompt: A hugely popular song came out three years ago. Why can't it join the National Recording Registry this year?

options.label: Recordings must be at least 10 years old
Only recordings made before 1970 qualify
options.rationale: The rule is an age of at least 10 years, not a cutoff year.

options.label: Only music recorded at the Library of Congress qualifies
options.rationale: Recordings from anywhere can be chosen.

options.label: Popular songs are never chosen
options.rationale: Hits like "Respect" are on the list.

questions.explanation: A recording has to be at least 10 years old, as well as culturally, historically or aesthetically significant.

questions.prompt: From Level 71's recorded sound: what could Edison's phonograph do that Scott's phonautograph couldn't?

options.label: Record a whole song
options.rationale: Scott captured "Au Clair de la Lune" in 1860.

options.label: Turn sound into a visible trace
options.rationale: The phonautograph already did that on paper.

questions.explanation: Scott's machine drew sound but couldn't replay it. Edison's 1877 phonograph was the first to record and play back.

questions.prompt: From Level 73's rock and roll roots: who were among the style's first big stars?

options.label: British bands such as the Beatles
options.rationale: They came later, inspired by those stars.

options.label: Black artists such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Fats Domino
Classical pianists who switched to guitar
options.rationale: The first stars came out of rhythm and blues.

options.label: Opera singers from New York
options.rationale: The first stars came out of rhythm and blues.

questions.explanation: Early rock and roll's stars included Fats Domino, Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Bo Diddley, Black artists rooted in rhythm and blues.

questions.prompt: From Level 74's electric guitar physics: what does a vibrating steel string change inside a pickup?

options.label: The air pressure inside the guitar's body
options.rationale: A pickup works by magnetism, not air.

options.label: The tension of the guitar's neck
options.rationale: The neck isn't part of the pickup.

options.label: The magnetic field through a coil of wire
The temperature of the magnet
options.rationale: It's the changing magnetic field that makes the voltage.

questions.explanation: The moving string changes the magnetic field through the coil, and by Faraday's law that induces a voltage.
